Status (the drafting log’s opening line):

Status: LIONESS edges, network metrics, and pathway connectivity and crosstalk are, to first order and in practice, fixed quadratic functions of the sample’s own expression, so over repeated visits they describe, explain, and predict as the expression scores do; there is no correction (pilot-f) and no fix, only a diagnostic (compare with the expression terms); prediction with pathway metrics and real gene sets has not been piloted.

The seven paper-test answers are in the drafting log.

Abstract

Background. LIONESS builds a co-expression network for each sample, and network metrics of those networks, read by pathway, are used as personal markers that should track a patient over repeated visits. What these metrics measure has not been derived.

Results. A Pearson LIONESS edge is an exact function of the cohort correlation and the sample’s own standardized expression, and a pathway’s connectivity and crosstalk are, to first order, the squared pathway score and the product of two scores. In simulated children followed over visits, every network metric, among them degree, betweenness, transitivity, and the numbers of edges and nodes, was as stable as the same metric on the first-order network (largest difference 0.0024); connectivity and crosstalk had \(R^2\) of at least 0.99999 on their expression terms, and the residual’s stability was at most 0.044 once fourth-order terms were added. Pathway scores predicted same-visit activity, with power up to 0.80, while LIONESS metrics were declared predictive in no replicate at any effect and were equivalent to first-order metrics in every replicate.

Conclusions. The stability of a LIONESS network over a person’s visits is the stability of the person’s expression. A network metric should be compared with the expression terms of its closed form before it is read as co-expression.

1 Introduction

Blood is sampled again and again in people with lupus, to follow a disease that flares and remits [1]. A gene network for each sample promises to show how a patient’s co-expression changes from one visit to the next, beyond how much each gene is expressed. LIONESS builds such a network for each sample of a cohort: it compares the co-expression network of all samples with the network of all samples but one, and assigns the scaled difference to the sample left out [2]. With Pearson correlation as the network, the default of its R implementation, every sample receives one weight for every pair of genes [3]. In the paper that introduced lionessR, single-sample networks of bone tumours were built in this way, edges whose weights differed between patients with short and long metastasis-free survival were selected, and limma tested them, beside a separate test of expression levels [3]. A difference in a sample’s edge is read there as a difference in how that sample adds to the co-expression of the two genes. Co-expression is summarized by gene sets in two established ways: cohort networks by module eigengenes and module connectivity [4], and blood transcriptomes by fixed module repertoires [5]. For a single-sample network, the natural summaries of a pathway are the mean edge among its genes, its connectivity, and the mean edge between its genes and those of a second pathway, their crosstalk.

Repeated blood samples differ in expression between people and within a person over time. Blood gene expression is partly specific to the individual [6], the interferon signature of lupus is stable within patients [7], and cell composition drives much of the co-expression seen in bulk data [8]. A Pearson LIONESS edge between genes \(i\) and \(j\) in sample \(q\) is, to first order in \(1/N\) for a cohort of \(N\) samples, a function of that sample’s own standardized expression \(z_{qi}\) and \(z_{qj}\) and of the cohort correlation \(r_{ij}\): \[ e_{qij} \approx r_{ij} + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2}\left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right). \] The product term is the single-sample correlation of earlier work [9]. Averaged over the pairs of a pathway, the product term becomes the square of the pathway’s summed expression, so a sample’s connectivity follows its pathway score. In a network built from all samples, module networks are approximately factorizable, and a gene’s connectivity has a counterpart computed from the module eigengene [10]. That result concerns connectivity across the genes of one cohort network. What has not been derived is the closed form of one sample’s pathway connectivity and crosstalk, and what it implies for their stability over a person’s visits and for their value as predictors.

This paper derives the exact closed form of a Pearson LIONESS edge and, from it, what the usual network metrics of a single-sample network measure, read through pathways: connectivity, crosstalk, total edge weight, strength, degree, betweenness, transitivity, and the numbers of edges and nodes. It then asks three questions. How much do these LIONESS metrics change across a person’s visits? Is that change the change in the person’s own expression, as the closed forms say? Do the LIONESS metrics identify a person and predict disease activity, at the same visit and at the next, better than pathway expression scores, and differently from the same metrics computed on the first-order form of the edges? The Methods give the closed forms and a diagnostic that compares a network metric with its expression terms. A simulation study of repeated visits varies how stable and how strong a pathway’s driving factor is, the pathway’s size, and person-specific co-expression. The application follows children with lupus over repeated visits.

2 Methods

2.1 The estimand and the procedure

A user who builds a LIONESS network for a blood sample reads it as the co-expression specific to that sample, and reads a network metric of it, such as the connectivity of the interferon genes, as how tightly that pathway’s genes move together in that person at that visit. Over repeated visits, the stability of the metric is then read as the stability of the person’s network. The procedure is the following. For a cohort of \(N\) samples, let \(r_{ij}\) be the Pearson correlation of genes \(i\) and \(j\) over all samples and \(r^{(-q)}_{ij}\) the correlation without sample \(q\). The LIONESS edge of sample \(q\) is \[ e_{qij} = N r_{ij} - (N - 1)\, r^{(-q)}_{ij} \] [2]. For a pathway \(A\) of \(m_A\) genes and a second pathway \(B\), the connectivity, the crosstalk, the total edge weight over all \(p\) genes, and the strength of gene \(i\) are \[ \begin{aligned} W_{qA} &= \binom{m_A}{2}^{-1} \sum_{i < j \in A} e_{qij}, \\ X_{qAB} &= \frac{1}{m_A m_B} \sum_{i \in A} \sum_{j \in B} e_{qij}, \\ T_q &= \sum_{i < j} e_{qij}, \\ s_{qi} &= \sum_{j \ne i} e_{qij}. \end{aligned} \] The graph metrics use the graph \(G_q\) that keeps the pairs with \(\lvert e_{qij}\rvert\) above a threshold, either fixed or chosen so that a fixed share of pairs is kept: the number of edges and of nodes (genes with at least one edge) of \(G_q\), its transitivity (the share of connected triples that close into triangles), and each gene’s degree and betweenness, the latter with distance \(1/\lvert e_{qij}\rvert\). Gene-level metrics are averaged over the genes of each pathway.

2.2 What the procedure estimates

Every LIONESS edge is an exact function of the cohort correlation and the sample’s own standardized expression. With \(z_{qi}\) the expression of gene \(i\) in sample \(q\) standardized over all \(N\) samples (divisor \(N\)) and \(\varepsilon = 1/(N - 1)\), removing sample \(q\) gives (supplement, S1.1) \[ \begin{aligned} r^{(-q)}_{ij} &= \frac{r_{ij} - \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj}}{\sqrt{(1 - \varepsilon z_{qi}^2)(1 - \varepsilon z_{qj}^2)}}, \\ e_{qij} &= N r_{ij} - (N - 1)\, r^{(-q)}_{ij}. \end{aligned} \] Expanding in \(\varepsilon\) gives the first-order form and a remainder of order \(\varepsilon\) that is a polynomial of degree four in \(z_{qi}\) and \(z_{qj}\) (S1.2): \[ e_{qij} = r_{ij} + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2}\left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right) + O(\varepsilon). \] Summing the first-order form over the pairs of a pathway gives the connectivity and crosstalk as linear functions of three expression terms each (S1.3). With \(S_A = \sum_{i \in A} z_{qi}\), \(Q_A = \sum_{i \in A} z_{qi}^2\), \(R^B_i = \sum_{j \in B, j \ne i} r_{ij}\), and \(C_A = m_A (m_A - 1)/2\), \[ \begin{aligned} W_{qA} &\approx \bar r_A + \frac{S_A^2 - Q_A}{2 C_A} - \frac{1}{2 C_A} \sum_{i \in A} R^A_i z_{qi}^2, \\ X_{qAB} &\approx \bar r_{AB} + \frac{S_A S_B}{m_A m_B} - \frac{1}{2 m_A m_B} \Big( \sum_{i \in A} R^B_i z_{qi}^2 + \sum_{j \in B} R^A_j z_{qj}^2 \Big), \end{aligned} \] where \(\bar r_A\) and \(\bar r_{AB}\) are the mean cohort correlations within \(A\) and between \(A\) and \(B\). The connectivity is, up to small terms, the squared pathway score \((S_A/m_A)^2\), and the crosstalk the product of two pathway scores. The total edge weight is the same sum over all genes, and the strength of gene \(i\) is \(R_i + z_{qi}(S - z_{qi}) - \tfrac{1}{2} R_i z_{qi}^2 - \tfrac12 \sum_{j \ne i} r_{ij} z_{qj}^2\), with \(S\) and \(R_i\) over all genes (S1.4). The graph metrics have no closed form, but they are functions of the edges, and so of the same standardized expression. A metric is therefore stable over a person’s visits to the extent that the person’s expression terms are: the squared score of a pathway driven by a factor with within-person intraclass correlation \(\kappa\) has intraclass correlation \(\kappa^2\) when the factor is normal (S1.5).

2.3 The fix or the diagnostic

Two checks tell a user whether a LIONESS metric carries anything beyond the sample’s expression. The first recomputes the metric on the first-order form of the edges, the network the closed form predicts from expression alone, and compares the two metrics’ stability over visits and their predictions. The second regresses connectivity and crosstalk over samples on their three first-order expression terms, then with the fourth-order terms of the remainder added (\(S_A^4\), \(S_A^2 Q_A\), \(Q_A^2\), and \(\sum_{i \in A} z_{qi}^4\) for connectivity; the corresponding products for crosstalk), and reports the \(R^2\) and the stability of the residual. A metric that matches its first-order version, and whose residual is not stable, measures expression.

2.4 Data

The application uses the longitudinal study of children with systemic lupus erythematosus of [1], Gene Expression Omnibus series GSE65391, whole-blood expression on the Illumina HumanHT-12 array with disease activity (SLEDAI) recorded at every visit. The analysis keeps the 131 children with two or more visits, 897 visits in all, and the authors’ split into training and test children. Pathways are modules of the BloodGen3 repertoire, built from co-clustering in blood transcriptomes of sixteen immunological and physiological states [5], taken from its R package [11]. TO CONFIRM: the download of the module list and the minimum module size

2.5 Software and reproducibility

The code is organized as a research compendium [12]: an R package whose functions are documented and tested, analysis scripts that call those functions and write every result to a results folder, and this manuscript, which reads only from that folder, so that every number, table, and figure in it is computed from the saved results when the document is rendered. Each simulation cell has its own random seed, derived from the design table, and the per-replicate results are saved rather than summaries. The software and package versions used are recorded with the results.

The analyses used R version 4.6.2 (2026-10-29), with glmnet [13] for the elastic net and igraph for the graph metrics.

3 Simulation study

3.1 Design

The simulation study is reported in the ADEMP structure [14]: aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, and performance measures, with a Monte Carlo standard error for every reported rate and average.

The study has three aims, the paper’s questions: how stable over a person’s visits each LIONESS metric is (aim 1); whether that stability equals the stability of the same metric on the first-order network, and whether connectivity and crosstalk are their expression terms (aim 2); and whether LIONESS metrics identify a person and predict activity better than pathway scores, or differently from first-order metrics (aim 3).

Every simulated cohort had 131 people, the number of children with two or more visits in the application, and ninety or more genes in six pathways. Four pathways each loaded on their own factor, a person level plus a visit deviation: an interferon-like pathway, whose factor’s within-person intraclass correlation, loading, and size were varied, and neutrophil-like, lymphocyte-like, and plasmablast-like pathways with loading 0.60 and intraclass correlations 0.41, 0.48, and 0.39, the values measured in the application for the neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages and for disease activity. A fifth pathway had a noise correlation that differed between people by up to the spread \(\tau\) (person-specific co-expression), and a sixth had a fixed noise correlation. Every gene carried a person level of variance 0.50 and unit normal noise, and the factors were independent. Each visit had an activity score: the activity effect \(\beta\) times the mean of the interferon and plasmablast factors, plus a person level and visit noise with within-person intraclass correlation 0.39. Study S1 varied one factor at a time around a base setting at the measured values (Table 1), and added a null setting with no stable factor and no person-specific co-expression, where every residual stability is zero. Study S2 used the base setting with 5 activity effects, the first zero, which gives the tests’ type I error and power.

The estimands were the intraclass correlation over visits of every metric, on the LIONESS network and on its first-order form, and their difference; for connectivity and crosstalk, the \(R^2\) on the expression terms of first and of fourth order and the stability of each residual; fingerprinting accuracy, the share of people whose second-visit metrics correlate most with their own first-visit metrics [15]; and the concordance of predictions of activity with the observed activity. The graph metrics used the fixed threshold \(\lvert e_{qij}\rvert > 1\) and, separately, the 5 percent of pairs with the largest \(\lvert e_{qij}\rvert\). Three feature sets were compared: A, the metrics of the LIONESS network; B, the six pathway scores (mean standardized expression) and their squares; and C, the metrics of the first-order network. Each predicted activity by a Gaussian elastic net with mixing 0.50 [13], the penalty chosen by inner cross-validation, in 5-fold cross-validation with all visits of a person in one fold; next-visit prediction used the features and activity of one visit for the activity of the next, with the current activity unpenalized, against a regression on the current activity alone (\(R_0\)). A concordance was declared above one half when the lower 5 percent quantile of 200 bootstrap resamples of people exceeded one half, and two feature sets were declared equivalent when the 90 percent bootstrap interval of their difference lay within \(\pm 0.05\). Each setting had 100 replicates in the production design, which give a Monte Carlo standard error of a few thousandths for a stability and at most 0.05 for a rejection rate.

3.2 Results

3.2.1 LIONESS metrics changed from visit to visit

Every LIONESS metric changed from visit to visit, and none was stable. In the base setting, the stability over visits was 0.274 (MCSE 0.022) for interferon connectivity, 0.227 (MCSE 0.013) for the interferon genes’ degree, 0.099 (MCSE 0.013) for their betweenness, 0.045 (MCSE 0.009) for transitivity, 0.127 (MCSE 0.008) for the number of edges, 0.087 (MCSE 0.013) for the number of nodes, and 0.083 (MCSE 0.010) for the total edge weight (Figure 7). Single interferon edges had a mean stability of 0.150 (MCSE 0.005). The network of one simulated child looked different at two visits (Figure 1, Figure 2), and so did its pathway summary (Figure 3, Figure 4). Across children, interferon connectivity and the mean degree of the interferon genes rose and fell over the six visits without a consistent order (Figure 5, Figure 6). Fingerprinting accuracy was 0.018 for the LIONESS metrics and 0.034 for the pathway scores, against 0.01 by chance.

3.2.2 The stability of LIONESS metrics was the stability of expression

Each LIONESS metric was exactly as stable as the same metric on the first-order network: over every metric and every setting of study S1, the stability on the LIONESS network differed from the stability on the first-order network by at most 0.0024 (Figure 7, Table 2). Connectivity and crosstalk were linear in their first-order expression terms, with \(R^2\) at least 0.99999. Interferon connectivity followed the squared interferon score closely in one cohort (correlation 0.973, Figure 8), and its stability followed that of the squared score along the gradient of the interferon factor’s stability (Figure 9): 0.274 (MCSE 0.022) against 0.286 (MCSE 0.022) in the base setting and 0.644 (MCSE 0.012) against 0.684 (MCSE 0.012) at the most stable factor. The residual after the first-order terms was stable only when the factor was: its stability was 0.244 (MCSE 0.051) at the most stable factor. With the fourth-order terms added, the residual’s stability was at most 0.044 over every connectivity, crosstalk, and setting.

3.2.3 LIONESS metrics did not predict beyond expression

The LIONESS metrics predicted neither same-visit nor next-visit activity beyond what expression gave. Same-visit activity was predicted by the pathway scores, whose superiority test declared a concordance above one half in a share of replicates that rose from 0.00 with no effect to 0.80 (Figure 10). The LIONESS metrics and the first-order metrics were declared above one half in no replicate at any effect, and their concordance stayed below one half, between 0.464 and 0.477 (Table 3). The LIONESS metrics were declared equivalent to the first-order metrics in every replicate, for same-visit and next-visit activity alike. For next-visit activity, every feature set reached the concordance of the current activity alone (0.618 to 0.632).

4 Application

4.1 Data and comparison

The application follows the 131 children of GSE65391 with two or more visits. In these children the interferon score had a within-child intraclass correlation of 0.55, the base of the simulation’s gradient, and SLEDAI one of 0.39. TO CONFIRM: the BloodGen3 module list must be downloaded before the LIONESS networks of these children are computed; the claims of protocol.md, section 7, are pre-registered for it

4.2 What the application will show

The application tests whether a user who reads a child’s LIONESS network metrics over visits learns anything that the child’s module expression does not already say. TO CONFIRM: the analysis has not been run

5 Discussion

A Pearson LIONESS edge is an exact function of the cohort correlation and the sample’s own standardized expression, and its first-order form keeps nearly all of it. Every network metric built on the edges, read whole or by pathway, inherited that: in simulated children followed over visits, each metric was exactly as stable as the same metric on the first-order network, connectivity and crosstalk were their expression terms, and the stable part that remained beyond first order was the next-order expression term. Pathway connectivity was more stable than single edges because it averaged the edges into a squared pathway score. For a user, a change in a child’s LIONESS network from one visit to the next is a change in that child’s expression, and a network metric should be compared with the expression terms of its closed form before it is read as co-expression. LIONESS metrics also lost the sign of expression: activity driven by a factor’s level was predicted by pathway scores, while the metrics, which carry squared scores, did not predict it. Table 4 sets these results beside earlier work.

The study has limits. The simulation used disjoint pathways of equal size, independent factors, normal noise, and equal numbers of visits; real gene sets overlap and real visits are irregular. Person-level differences in gene levels were independent across genes. The thresholds of the graph metrics were one fixed value and one proportion. The application has not yet been run. TO CONFIRM: the supervisor’s confirmation of the re-scope and of the paper’s message

Several questions were left out on purpose. Lupus was not compared with rheumatoid arthritis or with healthy controls, single-sample methods other than LIONESS were not studied, and drug effects, ancestry, sex, and subtypes were not modelled. No dataset was merged with another study.

The expression data are Gene Expression Omnibus series GSE65391. The code is organized as a research compendium [12]. TO CONFIRM: the repository URL

Supplementary note S1

This note derives the closed forms the paper rests on. A Pearson LIONESS edge turns out to be an exact function of two things: the correlation of the two genes over the cohort, and the sample’s own standardized values of the two genes. Its first-order form, and the connectivity, crosstalk, strength, and total edge weight built from it, are then sums of products of the sample’s own expression. The last result says how stable a squared factor is over visits.

Throughout, \(N\) is the number of samples, \(z_{qi}\) the expression of gene \(i\) in sample \(q\) standardized over all \(N\) samples with divisor \(N\) (so \(\sum_q z_{qi} = 0\), \(\sum_q z_{qi}^2 = N\), and \(\sum_q z_{qi} z_{qj} = N r_{ij}\)), and \(\varepsilon = 1/(N - 1)\).

S1.1 The exact LIONESS edge

The correlation of genes \(i\) and \(j\) without sample \(q\) is \[ \begin{aligned} \bar z^{(-q)}_i &= -\varepsilon z_{qi}, \\ \sum_{p \ne q} (z_{pi} - \bar z^{(-q)}_i)(z_{pj} - \bar z^{(-q)}_j) &= N r_{ij} - z_{qi} z_{qj} - (N - 1)\varepsilon^2 z_{qi} z_{qj} = N r_{ij} - N \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj}, \\ \sum_{p \ne q} (z_{pi} - \bar z^{(-q)}_i)^2 &= N - N \varepsilon z_{qi}^2, \\ r^{(-q)}_{ij} &= \frac{r_{ij} - \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj}}{\sqrt{(1 - \varepsilon z_{qi}^2)(1 - \varepsilon z_{qj}^2)}}. \end{aligned} \] Line 1: the standardized values sum to 0, so without \(z_{qi}\) the other \(N - 1\) sum to \(-z_{qi}\). Line 2: the centred cross-product is the raw one, \(N r_{ij} - z_{qi} z_{qj}\), minus \((N - 1)\) times the product of the means; \(1 + \varepsilon = N \varepsilon\). Line 3: line 2 with \(j = i\). Line 4: a correlation does not change under the affine map from expression to standardized expression, and the factor \(N\) cancels. The LIONESS edge \(e_{qij} = N r_{ij} - (N - 1) r^{(-q)}_{ij}\) is therefore a function of \(r_{ij}\), \(z_{qi}\), and \(z_{qj}\) alone. The paper uses this in the Methods; LionessEdgesClosedForm() is tested equal to leave-one-out LIONESS in tests/testthat/test-lioness.R.

S1.2 The first-order form and its remainder

With \(u = z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\) and \(v = \tfrac38 (z_{qi}^4 + z_{qj}^4) + \tfrac14 z_{qi}^2 z_{qj}^2\), \[ \begin{aligned} \left[(1 - \varepsilon z_{qi}^2)(1 - \varepsilon z_{qj}^2)\right]^{-1/2} &= 1 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} u + \varepsilon^2 v + O(\varepsilon^3), \\ (N - 1)\, r^{(-q)}_{ij} &= \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}(r_{ij} - \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj})\left(1 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} u + \varepsilon^2 v\right) + O(\varepsilon^2) \\ &= \tfrac{r_{ij}}{\varepsilon} - z_{qi} z_{qj} + \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2} u + \varepsilon\left(r_{ij} v - \tfrac12 z_{qi} z_{qj} u\right) + O(\varepsilon^2), \\ e_{qij} &= r_{ij} + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2} u + \varepsilon\left(\tfrac12 z_{qi} z_{qj} u - r_{ij} v\right) + O(\varepsilon^2). \end{aligned} \] Line 1: \((1 - a)^{-1/2} = 1 + a/2 + 3a^2/8 + O(a^3)\) for each factor, multiplied out; it holds because \(z_{qi}^2 \le N - 1\). Lines 2 and 3: S1.1 multiplied by \(N - 1 = 1/\varepsilon\) and expanded. Line 4: \(N r_{ij} - r_{ij}/\varepsilon = r_{ij}\). The first-order form is the part without \(\varepsilon\); the remainder is \(\varepsilon\) times a polynomial of degree four in \(z_{qi}\) and \(z_{qj}\). The paper uses this for the diagnostic’s fourth-order terms; the test in test-lioness.R checks that the gap to the first-order form shrinks as \(N\) grows.

S1.3 Connectivity and crosstalk

For disjoint pathways \(A\) and \(B\), with \(S_A\), \(Q_A\), \(R^B_i\), and \(C_A\) as in the Methods, the first-order form summed over pairs gives \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i < j \in A} z_{qi} z_{qj} &= \tfrac12 \left(S_A^2 - Q_A\right), \\ \sum_{i < j \in A} \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2} \left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right) &= \tfrac12 \sum_{i \in A} R^A_i z_{qi}^2, \\ \sum_{i \in A} \sum_{j \in B} z_{qi} z_{qj} &= S_A S_B, \\ \sum_{i \in A} \sum_{j \in B} \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2} \left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right) &= \tfrac12 \Big(\sum_{i \in A} R^B_i z_{qi}^2 + \sum_{j \in B} R^A_j z_{qj}^2\Big). \end{aligned} \] Line 1: \(S_A^2\) counts each product of two different genes twice and each square once. Line 2: each \(z_{qi}^2\) appears once for every other gene \(j\) of \(A\), weighted by \(r_{ij}\). Lines 3 and 4: the same over the pairs between \(A\) and \(B\). Dividing by \(C_A\) and \(m_A m_B\), and adding the mean correlations, gives the Methods’ formulas for \(W_{qA}\) and \(X_{qAB}\). The paper uses them in the Methods and the diagnostic; KnownAnswerChecksG() and tests/testthat/test-pathways.R check that first-order connectivity and crosstalk equal them to rounding.

S1.4 Strength and total edge weight

With \(S\) and \(R_i = \sum_{j \ne i} r_{ij}\) over all \(p\) genes, \[ \begin{aligned} s_{qi} &= \sum_{j \ne i} \Big[r_{ij} + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2}\left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right)\Big] = R_i + z_{qi}(S - z_{qi}) - \tfrac12 R_i z_{qi}^2 - \tfrac12 \sum_{j \ne i} r_{ij} z_{qj}^2, \\ T_q &= \sum_{i < j} r_{ij} + \tfrac12 \left(S^2 - Q\right) - \tfrac12 \sum_i R_i z_{qi}^2. \end{aligned} \] Line 1: the first-order form summed over the other genes. Line 2: S1.3 with \(A\) the whole gene set. The paper uses these in the Methods; tests/testthat/test-study.R checks the strength formula on first-order edges.

S1.5 The stability of a squared factor

Let a person’s factor at a visit be \(F = U + V\), with \(U \sim N(0, \kappa)\) the person’s level, \(V \sim N(0, 1 - \kappa)\) the visit’s deviation, independent, so that \(F\) has intraclass correlation \(\kappa\). Then \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{E}(F^2 \mid U) &= U^2 + 1 - \kappa, \\ \operatorname{Var}\{\operatorname{E}(F^2 \mid U)\} &= \operatorname{Var}(U^2) = 2\kappa^2, \\ \operatorname{Var}(F^2) &= 2, \\ \operatorname{ICC}(F^2) &= \kappa^2. \end{aligned} \] Line 1: \(\operatorname{E}(V) = 0\) and \(\operatorname{E}(V^2) = 1 - \kappa\). Line 2: the variance of the square of a normal variable with variance \(\kappa\) is \(2\kappa^2\). Line 3: \(F \sim N(0, 1)\). Line 4: the between-person share of the variance. The paper uses this to read the stability of connectivity as that of a squared expression score; KnownAnswerChecksD() checks it by simulation.
